title.en: Uvikiak: The Mock-Song of the Murderers
title.zh: 烏維基亞克：兇手的嘲歌

region.en: Northern coast journey and the murderers' dancing ground
region.zh: 北航海岸與兇手們的舞場

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; one of the oldest manuscripts, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 34 'Uvikiak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Travelling north, Uvikiak's son is found dead at the landing-place — pierced beneath the arms, eyes covered with his own entrails. Following the murders from camp to camp, he hears first the mock-song ('they laughed and scorned him'), then a boat's crew singing very sadly about the young man they had killed. At the murderers' settlement, hidden under a keel-upturned boat and over the dancing-hill, he and his daughters seize two flushed, undressed young men fresh from the song, kill them, and set them up in exactly the position of the son — hearing the cry of vengeance from hiding before escaping home to the south.
summary.zh: 北行途中，烏維基亞克的兒子陳屍於約定的登岸處——腋下貫穿銳器、雙眼被自己的腸臟覆蓋。一路追蹤，他先聽見營中的嘲歌——『他們笑他、辱他』——後又聽得一船之人悲唱那被他們殺死的少年。到了兇手的聚落，父女藏身於翻扣的船底與舞山之後，擒住兩名剛唱完歌、汗流滿面赤身而來的年輕人，依其子之狀陳屍示眾，隱身聽得復仇的喊叫，方才安然南歸。

sensitivity.note: Graphic murder description recorded as told in the 1875 source. The mock-song as evidence motif recurs in Greenlandic feud tales.

passages.text: Uvikiak was travelling to the north, accompanied by one son and two daughters. Whenever he came to a favourable shore the son kayaked ahead of them, and when the others came up to the spot they had fixed to land upon, he was already standing in waiting. They generally remained on land for the night and travelled further the next day; in the evening the son roamed ahead, as usual, to await them ashore — but when they landed and looked for him he was not to be seen. They pushed off again, and having doubled a point of land and got into a bay, they saw his lifeless body, standing erect, pierced with sharp weapons beneath his arms, and his eyes covered with some of his entrails. At this sight his father groaned with despair, and left the place to get hold of the murderers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 34 'Uvikiak'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Some way off he observed some tents, and went and asked, 'Have ye seen no travellers pass by this way?' — 'To be sure we have: yesterday a boat passed by; they were singing some kind of mock song about a young lad whose eyes had been covered with his entrails, and at which they laughed and scorned him.' At this report the father was still more provoked; always lamenting the lost one, they continued their journey of discovery, making inquiries at several other places, where they always got the same information, that a boat had newly passed by. Uvikiak still travelled on, with his wife and his two daughters, never now coming on shore in the night. At last they again reached some tents, and on making the usual inquiries got the answer that a boat had lately passed by, the crew of which were singing very sadly about a young man they had killed — and the wrath of the old Uvikiak somewhat subsided at their mild words.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 34 'Uvikiak'; not verbatim.

passages.text: They continued their journey for several days without being able to sleep in the night for excitement; but at length they set foot on the spot where lived the murderers. They put in and landed somewhat at the back of their dwelling-place, and having got the boat on shore, placed it keel upwards, and gathered crowberry plants and grass to cover it up with; Uvikiak's wife betook herself under the boat, while he himself went away with his daughters across the isthmus. They soon heard a noise, and listening on one of the nearest hills, just above the spot where they used to have dancing and other games, they heard distinctly that one of them was singing about Uvikiak's son. The song being finished, two young men came walking up-hill, flushed with heat and quite undressed; the new-comers at once inquired something about the singers — 'It is our master; he was just singing about a young man whom we happened to meet with down in the south, and killed — it was mighty amusing.' In a great rage Uvikiak instantly seized the one of them, and the daughters the other; they soon got the better of both, and having killed them, put them in exactly the same position as that in which they had seen Uvikiak's son, after which they hid themselves at a little distance. They had not to wait long before they heard a cry of vengeance; but their hiding-place was not discovered, and they escaped without any harm, and then returned to their home in the south.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 34 'Uvikiak'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Sun and the Moon: Sister's Fire, Brother's Smoke
title.zh: 日月神話：姊之焰與弟之煙

region.en: Old woman's house and the ascending skies

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; translated from one of the oldest manuscripts; also known at Point Barrow, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 35 'The Sun and the Moon', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Announced by snow-bunting, wheat-ear, and raven, a beautiful woman visits a lonely wife and tells the incest tale: courting in the dark, she sooted her hands to mark her lover and found her own brother's white jacket besmeared — cutting off her breasts, 'Since my body seems to please thee, pray take these and eat them.' Racing about the room with lit moss, they are lifted into the air; his light goes out, hers keeps burning — she has become the sun, on her way higher up the skies to give warmth to the orphans and make summer. One last look shows her back a mere skeleton.
summary.zh: 雪鳥、穗鵖與渡鴉依次報信後，一位美貌婦人造訪獨守的老嫗，自述亂倫之罪：黑夜中擇偶嬉戲，她以煙灰塗掌辨認意中人，竟發現哥哥的白袍沾滿灰黑——她割下雙乳：『既然我的身體合你心意，就把這個也吃了吧。』二人持燃苔追逐，忽被舉上長空；他的光熄了，她的光長明——她已成為太陽，正升向更高的天際，『好讓陽光溫暖孤兒們，為大地帶來夏天』。臨別一瞥，她的背影已是枯骨一副。

sensitivity.note: Incest and self-mutilation recorded as told in the 1875 source. Rink notes a Point Barrow version (John Simpson, surgeon of the Plover) with nearly the same words — evidence of the tale's circumpolar spread.

passages.text: An old married couple remained at home while their children travelled about all the summer. One day the wife was left alone as usual while the husband was out kayaking; on hearing something moving about close by, she hastened to hide beneath her coverlet, and after a little while, when she ventured to peep above it, saw a little snow-bunting hopping about on the floor and chirping, 'Another one will soon enter, who is going to tell thee something.' In a little while she was alarmed by a still greater noise, and looking up again beheld a kusagtak (the wheat-ear), likewise hopping on the floor and singing, 'Somebody shall soon enter and tell thee something.' It left the room, and was soon followed by a raven; but soon after it had gone she heard a sound like the steps of people, and this time saw a very beautiful woman who entered.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 35 'The Sun and the Moon'; not verbatim.

passages.text: On asking whence she came, the stranger told: 'In bygone days we often used to assemble in my home to divert ourselves at different plays and games, and in the evening, when it was all ended, the young girls generally remained out, and the young men used to pursue and court us; but we could never manage to recognise them in the dark. One night I was curious to know the one who had chosen me, and so I went and daubed my hands with soot before I joined the others. When our play had come to an end, I drew my hands along his back, and left him, and was the first who entered the house. The young people came in, one after another undressed, but for some time I observed no marks. Last of all my brother entered, and I saw at once that the back of his white jacket was all besmeared with soot. I took a knife, and sharpened it, and proceeded to cut off my two breasts, and gave him them, saying, Since my body seems to please thee, pray take these and eat them.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 35 'The Sun and the Moon'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'He now began to speak indecently to me, and courted me more than ever, and while we raced about the room he caught hold of some bad moss and lit it, but I took some that was good, and also lit mine. He ran out, and I ran after him; but suddenly I felt that we were lifted up, and soared high up in the air. When we got more aloft my brother's light was extinguished, but mine remained burning, and I had become a sun. Now I am on my way higher up the skies, that I may give warmth to the orphans' — going, the teller explains, to make summer. Finally she said, 'Now close thy eyes.' The woman turned her eyes downwards; but perceiving that she was about to leave the house, she gave her one look, and observed that at her back she was a mere skeleton. Soon after she had left the house the old husband returned.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 35 'The Sun and the Moon'; not verbatim.
